title: safe: agent contract — what is gated, how refusals look, how to get unblocked
intro: This machine routes package execution and installation through `safe`, a supply-chain safety net. If a package-manager command fails with a message starting with `safe:` or `safe run:`, it was refused BY POLICY — the toolchain is not broken.
one_rule: A refusal is policy, not breakage. Do not work around it: no direct node_modules/.bin calls of packages that failed to install, no alternate installers, no curl|sh. Relay the refusal and its `to allow:` command to the operator verbatim, wait, then retry the original command unchanged.

gated_surfaces.mechanism: Binaries are symlinked to `safe run`: packages run from a project node_modules/.bin (bare unversioned names, current or parent dir), an allowlist, a Podman sandbox, or not at all. A bare name for a gate-bound package-manager tool silently delegates to that tool's PATH wrapper; a missing or non-gate-bound target refuses.

gated_surfaces.surface: npm, pnpm, pnpx, yarn, bun, pip, pip3, uv, cargo, go, composer, mise
gated_surfaces.mechanism: PATH wrappers in ~/.local/bin exec `safe gate <tool>`, which audits install, update, and exec-style subcommands with `safe audit` before delegating to the real tool. This applies in every shell, not just interactive zsh.
Audited, confirmed install path (multi-manager). With no specs in a project directory it audits the project's dependencies instead.

audited_subcommands: Installs (install/add/ci/require and global variants), updates (update/up/upgrade, npm it), and exec-style fetch-and-run (npm exec|x, pnpm dlx, pnpx, yarn dlx, bun x, uv run --with|-w, uv tool run, go run <module>@<version>). npm aliases and command abbreviations that resolve to these gated routes are audited, including npm's camel-case normalization. Composer accepts only canonical install, update, require, reinstall, and create-project spellings plus the exact global proxy, case-insensitively as Symfony dispatches them; aliases and abbreviations targeting those gated commands refuse before delegation with both a canonical spelling and composer run-script escape hatch. An accepted gated Composer-global route scans its existing Unix global-home project and any effective first absolute --working-dir project; relative working directories refuse. A non-global install-class route (install, update, require, reinstall, or a package-less create-project) instead scans the project at its effective --working-dir/-d directory rather than the process cwd, and refuses if that directory exists but cannot be read; only a glued short-option working directory placed before the subcommand (composer -d<dir> install) stays fail-closed instead. Composer require requires at least one explicit package so interactive discovery cannot cross the audit boundary, and its value-taking options never count as packages. Composer reinstall re-fetches the locked tree and is audited as an install-class project scan. Composer create-project audits only its first positional package (the trailing directory and version positionals are never packages) plus any --require additions; a bare create-project inside an existing project scans it install-class, and with no package and no project it refuses so nothing is fetched unaudited. Safe preserves the original command token on every path that reaches delegation. An unrecognized space-form value flag before the accepted global nested command fails closed (escapable with --flag=value).
passthrough: No registry fetch, no gate: non-install subcommands (npm run, npm --version, ...), npm exec/npx of a bare unversioned name already in node_modules/.bin of the current or a parent directory (a versioned or aliased spec is still audited), pnpm exec and composer exec (project/vendor binaries only), uv run without --with, and go run of local paths. npx --no-install/--no is honored strictly: the local binary runs or the refusal is exit 100, never a registry fetch.
refusal_format: safe: BLOCKED <tool> <action> — <reason>; to allow: <operator command>; details: safe explain
refusal_note: The refusal is the FINAL stderr line in that shape. It may be preceded by the audit's own report and `safe audit:` hint lines — relay the BLOCKED line (plus any `safe audit:` hints) to the operator; the lines above it are supporting evidence, not the refusal.
preflight: Before proposing an install, an agent can check a spec directly: `safe audit package-audit <pkg>@<version> --ecosystem <eco>` (add `--json` for the receipt). It prints Socket, OSV, blocklist, and release-age lines, `VERDICT: GO|WARN|BLOCK`, next-step hints on WARN/BLOCK, and exits 0/10/20 — those are verdict codes, not refusals. Exit 30 is different in kind: the audit could not run, so there is no verdict and nothing was learned about the package. Socket is the primary behavioral tier: critical supply-chain-risk alerts BLOCK, while infrastructure failures WARN with a recovery path. The gate turns the same WARN into a refusal with exit 100 (unless an allow matches) and BLOCK into exit 104.

exit_codes.meaning: clean verdict (GO) from `safe audit package-audit`, or a gated command that passed and ran

`safe audit package-audit` verdict WARN (advisory affecting the resolved version, Socket behavioral risk short of a critical supply-chain-risk alert, custom source, unresolved version, or an audit-infrastructure failure — the per-scanner lines say which)
exit_codes.agent_action: Read the `safe audit:` hint lines: an infrastructure cause is breakage to escalate, an advisory cause is the gate working. Via the gate this same state refuses with exit 100.

exit_codes.meaning: `safe audit package-audit` verdict BLOCK (critical advisory affecting the resolved version, a known-malware `MAL-*` record, a Socket critical supply-chain-risk alert, or blocklist)
exit_codes.agent_action: Do not install. Via the gate this refuses with exit 104; the receipt carries the evidence. A BLOCK always rests on evidence about the package — when the audit could not run at all the code is 30, not 20.

exit_codes.meaning: `safe audit package-audit` could not produce a verdict at all — audit-infrastructure breakage (the verdict engine is missing, version-skewed, or failed; or the evidence could not be assembled). This is NOT a package finding and carries no evidence about the package.
exit_codes.agent_action: Do not read this as a refusal about the package, and do not retry the install. Repair the tooling: rerun install.sh, then `safe doctor`. Escalate to the operator if it persists. Via the gate this refuses with exit 100.

exit_codes.meaning: blocked by policy: an audit WARN with no matching allow entry, blocklist, fail-closed audit, or unrecognized/unsupported runner-native flags — the refusal line names which
exit_codes.agent_action: Relay the refusal line verbatim to the operator. Do not retry, do not reword the command.
The allowlist pins a different version than the one requested. Report both versions; re-pin is an operator decision.
Nothing an agent can do in this shell. Ask the operator to run it in their terminal.
Check the spec for a typo before escalating — this one is usually the caller's error.

The audit returned BLOCK. That can be a critical advisory affecting the resolved version, a known-malware or blocklist entry, a Socket critical supply-chain-risk alert, or a critical advisory safe could not tie to a resolved version — the reason is in the receipt. Inspect it, and use `safe report-fp <spec>` only when its resolved-version and advisory evidence are inconsistent with the refusal.

exit_codes.meaning: genuinely missing command (never a policy refusal)
exit_codes.agent_action: The command is not installed, or `safe` is missing from PATH. Report it; never treat it as a reason to bypass.

agent_rules: Treat any BLOCKED line as policy, not breakage; do not retry blind.

Relay the refusal line and its `to allow:` command to the operator verbatim. Trust escalations (safe run host-allow add/update/import) only work in the operator's interactive terminal — never attempt them yourself.
After the operator allows, retry the original command unchanged.

Exit 127 from a wrapped tool means a genuinely missing command (or a `safe` missing from PATH), never a policy block — the gate always refuses legibly with exit 100. Report a silent 127, don't bypass.
Never construct or request `<pkg>@latest`; use the pinned version the refusal names.
If the advisories do not affect the resolved version, run `safe report-fp <spec>` instead of arguing with the gate.

Preflight with `safe audit package-audit <pkg>@<version> --ecosystem <eco>` before proposing an install; its exit codes are verdicts (0/10/20), not refusals. Exit 30 means the audit could not run at all — repair the tooling, never read it as a verdict about the package.

version_resolution.rule: safe audits the version that will actually be installed, never the literal string `latest`. An unversioned spec is resolved through the registry first (dist-tag for installs, the max version satisfying the declared range for updates), and the advisory match is evaluated against that resolved version.
version_resolution.never_latest: Never suggest, request, or construct an allow entry for `<pkg>@latest`. Allow entries are pinned to resolved versions. A refusal that needs an allow will name the exact pinned version in its `to allow:` command — use that string as-is.
version_resolution.unresolvable: When resolution fails (a private registry, a git or workspace spec, a compound range), the verdict floors at WARN with reason `version_unresolved` and is never auto-allowed. Pin an exact version and retry.

escalation.situation: Audit backend is down or unauthenticated
escalation.signal: The refusal names a Socket auth failure, a rate limit, or a network error — not an advisory.
escalation.action: Escalate to the operator immediately. Do not park it, do not retry around it, do not treat it as a vulnerability finding. Recovery is usually `socket login` or a vault-injection fix; `safe doctor` checks the wiring. Exception: `PENDING (fresh release ...)` means Socket has not completed its first score; with clean OSV and blocklist evidence it is disclosed data availability, not backend breakage.

escalation.situation: A critical advisory affects the resolved version
escalation.signal: Exit 104 with an advisory ID and the resolved version.
escalation.action: This is the gate working. Report the advisory to the operator and propose a fixed version if one exists.

escalation.situation: The advisory does not affect the resolved version
escalation.signal: In the receipt (`--json`), an advisory listed as affecting carries a fixed bound at or below the resolved version — the advisory's own range data contradicts the verdict.
escalation.action: Suspected false positive. Run `safe report-fp <spec>` — it re-runs the check, saves the receipt, and writes a dated note in safe's inbox listing every advisory's fixed bound so the operator can apply the disqualifying test. Nothing auto-applies.

escalation.situation: A refusal carries BOTH an advisory hint and an infrastructure hint
escalation.signal: One `safe audit:` line offers a pinned allow command while another names a Socket/OSV failure as infrastructure breakage.
escalation.action: Infrastructure first: get the broken check fixed (or escalate it), then re-run — the verdict may change once full evidence is available. Only pursue the allow lane on a verdict computed with all checks working.

escalation.situation: A scanner is missing or broke
escalation.signal: The output names a missing or failed Socket check and the verdict degraded to WARN.
escalation.action: Coverage is missing, not a finding. Run `safe doctor` and report a present scanner that failed; do not read an infrastructure warning as a vulnerability.

report_fp.what_it_does: Re-runs the check as JSON, saves the receipt, and writes inbox/YYYY-MM-DD-<source>-fp-<slug>.md in safe's repo with the command it ran, its exit code, the resolved version, every advisory with its fixed bound, and the receipt path. It re-runs the check rather than capturing the original refusal, so quote that refusal to the operator yourself if it matters.
report_fp.contract: The note IS the escalation. Nothing auto-applies and no behaviour changes until the operator validates it.

allow_flows.command: safe run block list && safe run audit --blocked

allow_flows_note: Trust escalations require the operator's interactive terminal. `safe run host-allow add`, `update`, and `import` (without `--dry-run`) refuse in non-TTY shells with exit 102, so an agent can suggest the command but never execute it.
no_partial_load: Gating is executable-based: a wrapper either runs the full gate or is not on PATH at all. If `safe gate` cannot load its routing tables it refuses with the usual `safe: BLOCKED` line and exit 100 rather than delegating. A bare silent 127 therefore means the command genuinely is not installed — or that `safe` itself is missing from PATH, which is worth reporting.
harness_snippet:
## Package manager gates

This machine gates package execution/installation through `safe`. If a
command fails with a `safe: BLOCKED` / `safe run: BLOCKED` line or exit code
100–104, that is policy, not breakage: run `safe explain`, relay the refusal
and its `to allow:` command to the operator verbatim, and never bypass
(no direct node_modules/.bin calls, alternate installers, or curl|sh).
Suspected false positive: `safe report-fp <spec>`.
